title: 22. Interview: MySQL
summary: Interview Q&A for MySQL — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 MySQL interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. How does InnoDB's clustered index differ from PostgreSQL's heap+index design?
**Answer:** In InnoDB, the table's primary key IS the data — rows are stored in the leaves of a B+Tree ordered by PK. This is called a "clustered index." Secondary indexes (on `email`, `created_at`, etc.) don't point to the row directly; they store the PK value, so a secondary-index lookup requires two B+Tree descents: (1) find the PK by the secondary key, (2) find the row by PK in the clustered index. In PostgreSQL, the table is a "heap" (unordered set of rows), and every index (including the PK) points directly to the row's physical location (TID). One B+Tree descent suffices for any index lookup. Trade-offs: InnoDB's clustered index makes PK lookups and range scans on PK very fast (data is colocated), and PK queries are common (`WHERE user_id = ?`). But secondary-index lookups are slower (two descents), and updating a PK column rewrites the entire row (and all secondary indexes) — expensive. PostgreSQL's heap design means all indexes are equal (one descent), but range scans on PK aren't faster than on any other indexed column. Best practice for InnoDB: choose an auto-incrementing integer PK (inserts append to the B+Tree, no fragmentation) and avoid PK updates. Real-world: InnoDB's clustered PK is why MySQL is so fast on `WHERE id = ?` point lookups (a common web-app pattern); PostgreSQL catches up via covering indexes (`INCLUDE` clause).
**Visual:**
```
InnoDB (clustered PK):

  Secondary index         Clustered index (= data)
  +-------+-------+       +----+-----------+
  | email | PK    |       | PK | row data  |
  +-------+-------+       +----+-----------+
  | a@x   | 42    | ----> | 42 | alice,... |
  | b@x   | 17    |       | 17 | bob,...   |
  +-------+-------+       +----+-----------+
  Lookup by email: 2 B-tree descents (find PK, find row)

PostgreSQL (heap + indexes):

  Any index                Heap (data)
  +-------+--------+       +--------+------+
  | email | rowptr | ----> | rowptr | row  |
  +-------+--------+       +--------+------+
  Lookup by email: 1 B-tree descent + 1 heap fetch

Trade-offs:
  InnoDB: PK lookup fast, secondary lookup slower, PK update expensive
  PG:     all indexes equal, range scan on PK same as any other
```

### Q2. What is the difference between redo log and binlog in MySQL?
**Answer:** MySQL has two separate logs that look similar but serve different purposes. **Redo log** (InnoDB-specific, `ib_logfile`): records **physical page changes** at the engine level ("write bytes X to page Y"). Used for crash recovery — after a crash, InnoDB replays the redo log to restore data pages to their last-committed state. The redo log is circular (fixed size) and is per-InnoDB-engine. **Binlog** (server-level, `mysql-bin.000001` etc.): records **logical changes** (statement-based or row-based) at the server level. Used for replication (replicas consume the binlog) and PITR (replay binlog from a backup to a chosen timestamp). The binlog is append-only (not circular) and is per-MySQL-server. Why two logs? Historical reasons — InnoDB was a third-party engine added to MySQL, which already had its own binlog. The two-phase commit between them (prepare in InnoDB, write binlog, commit in InnoDB) ensures crash consistency between engine and server logs. The redo log ensures the engine is crash-safe; the binlog ensures replication is consistent. Trade-offs: (1) Both logs add I/O — every commit writes to both (with fsync depending on `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit` and `sync_binlog`). (2) The two-phase commit adds latency. (3) For replication, only the binlog is needed; the redo log is engine-local. Real-world: in MySQL 8.0+, the binlog can be written in parallel with the redo log (atomic write) reducing commit latency; earlier versions had stricter ordering.
**Visual:**
```
MySQL commit (two-phase between redo and binlog):

  T=0:  BEGIN; UPDATE users SET balance=900 WHERE id=42;
  T=1:  InnoDB modifies buffer pool (data page in memory)
  T=2:  InnoDB writes redo log: [page X offset Y bytes 0x...]
        fsync redo log (innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1)
  T=3:  PREPARE (mark txn as prepared in engine)
  T=4:  MySQL writes binlog: [ROW UPDATE users id=42 before=1000 after=900]
        fsync binlog (sync_binlog=1)
  T=5:  COMMIT (mark txn as committed in engine)
  T=6:  ack client "committed"

  Redo log: physical, engine-local, circular, crash recovery
  Binlog:   logical, server-level, append-only, replication+PITR

  Two-phase commit ensures both logs agree (no torn state on crash)
```

### Q3. What is GTID and why is it important for replication?
**Answer:** GTID (Global Transaction Identifier) is a unique ID assigned to every committed transaction in a MySQL replication topology. Format: `server_uuid:sequence_number` (e.g., `3E2F1A-aaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddddddddddd:42`). Before GTID (pre-5.6), replication was tracked by binlog file + position — "replica is at mysql-bin.000123:4567". This was fragile: if the primary failed over to a new primary with a different binlog sequence, the replica's position was meaningless and you had to manually compute the equivalent position on the new primary (painful and error-prone). With GTID, every transaction has a globally unique ID; a replica tracks "I've applied GTIDs 1-42 from server A, 1-99 from server B." Re-pointing a replica to a new primary is automatic: the new primary sends "all GTIDs the replica hasn't seen." Benefits: (1) **Simple failover** — Orchestrator, MaaS, and other tools automatically re-point replicas using GTID position. (2) **Easy replication topology changes** — adding a replica mid-topology: it asks "what GTIDs do you have that I don't?" and catches up. (3) **Prevents accidental data loss** — if a replica has a GTID that the primary doesn't, replication errors out (the replica has diverged). (4) **Crash-safe slaves** — MySQL 5.7+ stores replica position in a transactional table, so a replica crash doesn't lose position info. Trade-offs: (1) GTID must be enabled from the start of the topology (converting an existing non-GTID setup is involved). (2) Some statements aren't GTID-safe (`CREATE TABLE ... SELECT`, `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE` inside a transaction) and are restricted. (3) Slightly more overhead per transaction. Real-world: every modern MySQL deployment uses GTID; it's effectively mandatory for HA tooling.
**Visual:**
```
Without GTID (file:position):
  Primary A: mysql-bin.000123:4567
  Replica:   "I'm at mysql-bin.000123:4567"
  Primary A fails -> failover to Primary B (different binlog seq)
  Replica must compute: "B's binlog equivalent of A's 000123:4567?"
  -> manual, error-prone, often requires resync

With GTID:
  Primary A: GTID 3E2F1A:1 ... 3E2F1A:42 (then fails)
  Replica:   "I've applied 3E2F1A:1..42"
  Failover to Primary B (which was replica of A)
  Replica reconnects to B: "I have 3E2F1A:1..42"
  B: "OK, sending 3E2F1A:43 onwards (and my own 4F2B1C:1..)"
  Replica catches up automatically.

  Tools like Orchestrator use GTID for fully automatic failover
  (detect failure, elect primary, re-point all replicas via GTID)
```

### Q4. What is semi-synchronous replication and how does it differ from async?
**Answer:** MySQL's default replication is **asynchronous**: the primary commits and returns to the client immediately; the replica catches up later via the binlog stream. This is fast (no wait) but has a small data-loss window on failover — the last few committed transactions may not have reached the replica. **Semi-synchronous replication** (`rpl_semi_sync_master_enabled=ON`) requires the primary to wait for at least one replica to ack receipt of the binlog event before returning COMMIT to the client. This guarantees the transaction is on at least two hosts (zero data loss for committed transactions) at the cost of one network round-trip per commit (~1 ms LAN, more cross-region). Two modes: **AFTER_COMMIT** (older, 5.5) — primary commits locally, then waits for ack; if the primary crashes after commit but before ack, the client sees "committed" but the replica doesn't have it (potential data loss). **AFTER_SYNC** (5.7+, "lossless semi-sync") — primary waits for ack BEFORE committing locally; the primary and replica have the transaction or neither does. Use AFTER_SYNC. Trade-offs: (1) Commit latency += RTT to acking replica (1-5 ms same-DC). (2) If all replicas are unreachable, semi-sync degrades to async after `rpl_semi_sync_master_timeout` (default 10 s) to avoid blocking the primary indefinitely — this is a fail-safe, not a desired state. (3) Throughput impact: writes are serialized waiting for acks, so commit throughput drops. Real-world: Facebook, Slack, and most large MySQL deployments use semi-sync with 2-3 replicas; lossless mode (AFTER_SYNC) is the modern default.
**Visual:**
```
Async replication (default):
  Primary: BEGIN; ... COMMIT -> ack client immediately
  Replica: catches up later (lag = ms to seconds)
  Failure: last few commits may be lost (data loss window = lag)

Semi-sync replication (AFTER_SYNC, "lossless"):
  Primary: BEGIN; ... write binlog; send to replica
           wait for replica to ack "received"
           COMMIT locally; ack client
  Replica: received binlog event (not yet applied)
  Failure: replica has the binlog event, can apply it on promotion
           -> ZERO data loss for committed txns

  Latency cost: +1 RTT per commit (~1ms same-DC, ~50ms cross-region)
  Throughput: writes serialized on ack -> lower max QPS

  Fail-safe: if all replicas unreachable for >10s, degrade to async
             (avoid indefinite primary block)
```

### Q5. What is InnoDB Cluster and how does it compare to traditional primary/replica?
**Answer:** InnoDB Cluster is MySQL's integrated HA solution combining three components: (1) **Group Replication** — a multi-node replication group using Paxos-like consensus for writes; members coordinate, detect failures, elect new primaries automatically. Supports single-primary mode (one writer, others read-only — typical) or multi-primary mode (all nodes accept writes — risky, conflict-prone). (2) **MySQL Router** — a thin proxy that routes client traffic to the right node (primary for writes, any for reads); clients connect to the router, not directly to MySQL. (3) **MySQL Shell** — admin CLI for cluster setup, monitoring, failover. Compared to traditional primary/replica: (1) **Automatic failover** — Group Replication detects a failed primary and promotes a replica in 10-30 seconds, vs minutes for traditional (Orchestrator + manual). (2) **Strong consistency** — Group Replication uses consensus, so all members agree on every committed transaction; traditional async replication has lag and potential data loss. (3) **Read scale** — Router can route reads to any member; traditional has read replicas too. (4) **Write throughput** — Group Replication is capped by consensus (slower than async); traditional async primary can write faster. (5) **Member limit** — Group Replication supports max 9 members; traditional can have hundreds of replicas. (6) **Network requirements** — Group Replication requires low latency (<5ms) between members; traditional tolerates cross-region lag. Trade-offs: InnoDB Cluster is best for HA in a single region with <10 nodes and automatic failover needs; traditional primary/replica is better for cross-region DR, very high write throughput, or hundreds of read replicas. Real-world: many companies use both — InnoDB Cluster per region for HA, with traditional async cross-region replication for DR.
**Visual:**
```
InnoDB Cluster (single-region HA, <10 nodes):

  Client -> MySQL Router -> [Group Replication cluster]
                              +-- Primary (writes)
                              +-- Member 2 (reads)
                              +-- Member 3 (reads)
                              (Paxos consensus on every write,
                               automatic failover in 10-30s)

Traditional primary/replica (cross-region DR, many replicas):

  Region 1: Primary -> 5 replicas (semi-sync)
  Region 2: Replica (async, ~50ms lag, DR only)
  Region 3: Replica (async, ~100ms lag, DR only)

  Orchestrator watches -> manual or auto failover (minutes)

Choose InnoDB Cluster for:
  + single-region HA, automatic failover
  + strong consistency on every commit
  + read scale with router

Choose traditional for:
  + cross-region DR (low-latency consensus can't span regions)
  + very high write throughput (consensus caps QPS)
  + hundreds of read replicas (Group Replication max 9)
```

### Q6. What is Vitess and how does it enable horizontal sharding for MySQL?
**Answer:** Vitess is a database clustering system (originally built at YouTube, now a CNCF graduated project) that horizontally shards MySQL while presenting a single logical database to the application. Architecture: (1) **VTGate** — a proxy that accepts SQL from the application, parses it, routes it to the right shard(s), and merges results. The app sees one MySQL connection; VTGate handles the fan-out. (2) **VTTablet** — a sidecar process on each MySQL instance that handles query execution, schema management, and replication coordination. (3) **Topology service** — stores cluster metadata (shard map, schema, primary location) in etcd or ZooKeeper. (4) **VReplication** — Vitess's own replication engine, supporting resharding, online schema changes, and materialized views. Sharding: Vitess shards by a chosen key (e.g., `user_id`); VTGate routes `WHERE user_id = 42` to the right shard. Cross-shard queries (`SELECT * FROM users WHERE created_at > X`) fan out to all shards and merge. Resharding (splitting a shard into two, or moving data to a new shard) happens online via VReplication — no downtime. Schema migrations use VReplication to build a new table copy in the background, then atomic swap. Real-world: YouTube, Slack, Square, GitHub (via PlanetScale managed service) all run Vitess. PlanetScale is the commercial managed Vitess. Trade-offs: (1) Cross-shard transactions are limited (Vitess supports 2PC but discourages it). (2) Cross-shard JOINs are limited (VTGate can do some, but not all — application-level fan-out preferred). (3) Adds latency (~1 ms per query for the VTGate hop). (4) Operational complexity — Vitess has many moving parts. Real-world: Slack runs Vitess with 1000+ shards handling billions of messages.
**Visual:**
```
Vitess architecture (horizontal sharding for MySQL):

  App -> VTGate (proxy, parses SQL, routes by shard key)
         |
         +-- shard 0 (users 0-999):    Primary + 2 replicas
         +-- shard 1 (users 1000-1999): Primary + 2 replicas
         +-- shard 2 (users 2000-2999): Primary + 2 replicas
         +-- shard N ...

  VTGate routes:
    SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id = 42      -> shard 0 (single)
    SELECT * FROM users WHERE created_at > X    -> ALL shards (fan-out+merge)
    INSERT INTO users (user_id, ...) VALUES (42,...) -> shard 0

  Resharding (split shard 0 into 0a and 0b):
    VReplication copies rows to new shards in background
    Cutover: atomic, <1s of downtime
    No app changes (VTGate routes transparently)

  Topology (etcd): shard map, schema, primary locations

  Used by: YouTube, Slack, Square, GitHub (via PlanetScale)
```

### Q7. Why did Uber migrate from PostgreSQL back to MySQL (2016 blog post)?
**Answer:** Uber Engineering's 2016 post "Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL" cited four issues with PostgreSQL: (1) **MVCC bloat from update-heavy workloads** — PostgreSQL's MVCC creates a new row version on every UPDATE, bloating tables and indexes. For Uber's update-heavy workloads (driver location, trip status), autovacuum couldn't keep up, requiring frequent `VACUUM FULL` (which locks the table). InnoDB's in-place updates (with undo logs) avoid this. (2) **Replication limitations** — pre-PostgreSQL 10, logical replication required third-party tools (pglogical, Slony) and was painful; physical replication required same major version. MySQL's binlog-based logical replication was more flexible for their use cases (cross-version, cross-schema). (3) **Postgres connection model** — PostgreSQL forks a process per connection (~10 MB each), so 1000 connections = 10 GB just for backends. MySQL uses threads (~1 MB each), supporting more connections per instance. (4) **Engineering familiarity** — Uber's team knew MySQL better operationally. The post was controversial: PostgreSQL advocates argued the issues were operational (autovacuum tuning, PgBouncer for connections, upgrading to newer PostgreSQL with logical replication) rather than fundamental. Uber later wrote a 2018 post clarifying some of this. The takeaway: both databases work at scale; the choice often comes down to workload characteristics (update-heavy favors InnoDB) and operational familiarity. Real-world: many large companies use both — Uber uses PostgreSQL for some services (matching engine) and MySQL for others; the choice is per-service.
**Visual:**
```
Uber's 2016 reasons (PG -> MySQL):

  Issue                  | PostgreSQL (pre-10)         | MySQL InnoDB
  -----------------------|-----------------------------|----------------
  UPDATE behavior        | new row version (bloat)     | in-place + undo log
  Autovacuum             | struggles on heavy updates  | no equivalent (no bloat)
  Replication            | physical (same version)     | binlog (cross-version)
  Logical replication    | third-party (pglogical)     | native (binlog)
  Connection model       | process (~10MB each)        | thread (~1MB each)
  Familiarity            | lower                       | higher

  Counter-arguments (PG advocates):
    + autovacuum tuning solves bloat (lower scale_factor)
    + PgBouncer multiplexes connections (no need for 1000 backends)
    + PostgreSQL 10+ has native logical replication
    + PostgreSQL's MVCC gives stronger consistency (no phantom reads)

  Lesson: both work at scale; per-service choice based on workload
          (update-heavy -> InnoDB, JSONB/extensions -> PG)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Instagram needs to store 1 billion users' data on MySQL. How do you architect this?
**Answer:** Single MySQL can't handle 1B users (would be petabytes, write QPS in millions). Architecture (matching Instagram/Facebook's actual approach): (1) **Shard by user_id** — `shard_id = user_id % N` where N is the number of shards (start with 1024, can grow). Each shard is a separate MySQL primary + replicas. A user's profile, photos, follows, comments all live on the same shard (co-located). (2) **Cross-shard queries** — for "show my feed" (which requires fetching posts from users I follow, who may be on different shards), the app fans out to N shards in parallel and merges. Pre-compute feeds for active users (write amplification: when user X posts, fan-out writes to followers' feed caches). (3) **Schema per shard** — identical schema on every shard. (4) **Semi-sync + cross-region DR** — each shard has a primary in region 1, 2 semi-sync replicas in region 1, 1 async replica in region 2 (DR). (5) **Vitess or app-layer sharding** — Vitess (used by Slack, YouTube) handles shard routing transparently; app-layer sharding (Instagram's approach) puts the shard-map logic in the app. (6) **Connection pooling** — ProxySQL or MySQL Router per app instance, pool size 10-20 per shard. (7) **Schema migrations** — use `gh-ost` or `pt-online-schema-change` for online DDL (no table lock). (8) **Monitoring** — per-shard metrics (lag, QPS, slow queries), alerting on hot shards. Real-world: Facebook/Instagram run thousands of MySQL shards; Vitess is the modern alternative for new deployments.
**Visual:**
```
Instagram sharded MySQL architecture:

  App (shard-aware) -> shard map (user_id % 1024)
       |
       +-- shard 0:    MySQL Primary + 2 semi-sync + 1 DR replica
       +-- shard 1:    MySQL Primary + 2 semi-sync + 1 DR replica
       +-- ...
       +-- shard 1023: MySQL Primary + 2 semi-sync + 1 DR replica

  User 42 -> shard 42%1024 = 42
    - profile, photos, follows, comments all on shard 42

  Cross-shard: "show my feed"
    - I follow users on shards 7, 42, 100, 999
    - fan-out: parallel SELECT to 4 shards, merge by created_at DESC
    - OR pre-computed: when user 42 posts, write to followers' feed cache
      (write amplification, but feed reads are O(1))

  Per shard:
    - ProxySQL pool (size 20)
    - gh-ost for online schema changes
    - semi-sync for zero data loss
    - DR replica cross-region

  Vitess alternative: VTGate routes by shard key, app sees 1 DB
```

### Q2. Your MySQL primary failed; semi-sync replica has lag of 5 seconds. What's the data loss, and how do you fail over?
**Answer:** With **AFTER_SYNC** (lossless) semi-sync, the primary waits for the replica to ack receipt of the binlog event BEFORE committing locally. So any committed transaction on the primary has been received by the replica — **zero data loss**, even if the replica hasn't applied the events yet (the binlog events are durable on the replica; on promotion, the replica applies them before accepting new writes). The "5 seconds lag" means the replica is 5 seconds behind in *applying* events, but it has *received* all events the primary committed. Failover procedure: (1) **Detect failure** — Orchestrator or MaaS pings the primary; after N failures (3-10s), declare it down. (2) **Verify quorum** — ensure the primary is really down, not a network partition (Orchestrator uses consensus across observers). (3) **Pick the most-caught-up replica** — the replica with the highest GTID/applied position. (4) **Ensure the replica has drained** — wait for the replica to apply all received binlog events (the 5-second lag drains in ~5 seconds). (5) **Promote** — `STOP SLAVE; RESET SLAVE ALL;` then the replica accepts writes. (6) **Update routing** — ProxySQL/MySQL Router/Consul update to point at the new primary. (7) **Re-point other replicas** — they now stream from the new primary. (8) **Old primary recovery** — when the old primary comes back, it must be rejoined as a replica (fenced to prevent split-brain). Total downtime: 10-60 seconds. Data loss: zero (with AFTER_SYNC). If using **AFTER_COMMIT** semi-sync (older) or async, data loss could be up to the lag of the most-caught-up replica (5 seconds of committed transactions may be lost). Real-world: this is why AFTER_SYNC is the recommended semi-sync mode.
**Visual:**
```
MySQL primary failure with semi-sync (AFTER_SYNC, "lossless"):

  Primary (failed at T=10s):
    Committed txns: GTID 1..1000 (all acked by replica)
    Binlog stream: sent GTID 1..1005 (1005 not yet committed locally)

  Replica (5s lag, "applying" GTID 995):
    Received: GTID 1..1005 (durable in relay log)
    Applied:  GTID 1..995 (still applying 996..1005)
    -> 5s lag in apply, but ALL received events are safe

  Failover:
    T=10s: detect primary failure (3 failed pings)
    T=15s: pick replica, wait for drain (apply 996..1005, ~5s)
    T=20s: replica drained (applied all received events)
           STOP SLAVE; RESET SLAVE ALL;
           replica now accepts writes -> new primary
    T=22s: ProxySQL updates routing
    T=25s: app connects to new primary, writes resume

  Data loss: ZERO (AFTER_SYNC guarantees committed = received by replica)
  Downtime: ~15-25s (detection + drain + promote + reroute)

  If async replication: data loss = lag of best replica (5s of txns)
```

### Q3. A 500 GB MySQL table has bloated to 2 TB. How do you reclaim space online?
**Answer:** MySQL InnoDB doesn't release disk space back to the OS when rows are deleted — it marks the space as free for reuse, but the file stays the same size. To reclaim the space: (1) **`OPTIMIZE TABLE`** — MySQL's built-in command, but it actually does `ALTER TABLE ... ENGINE=InnoDB`, which rebuilds the table. On InnoDB, this **takes an exclusive lock** in older versions (5.6 and earlier), blocking reads and writes for the duration (hours on 2 TB). (2) **Online `ALTER TABLE`** (MySQL 5.6+) — most `ALTER TABLE` operations are "in-place" with concurrent DML allowed. `ALTER TABLE t ENGINE=InnoDB` (no-op rebuild) is in-place; you can read and write during the rebuild. But the rebuild creates a new copy of the table, doubling disk usage during the operation. (3) **`gh-ost`** (GitHub's online schema change tool) — creates a shadow table, copies rows in batches, captures concurrent changes via triggers (or binlog), and swaps atomically. No exclusive lock, controllable throttling. The industry standard for MySQL. (4) **`pt-online-schema-change`** (Percona Toolkit) — similar to gh-ost, older, trigger-based. (5) **InnoDB page compression** — `ROW_FORMAT=COMPRESSED` compresses pages on disk, effective for repetitive data. The 2 TB might compress to 500 GB. (6) **MyRocks (RocksDB engine)** — Facebook's compressed MySQL engine, 2-10x smaller than InnoDB. Migration is significant. Recommended approach: use `gh-ost` to rebuild the table online with no downtime, then evaluate page compression or MyRocks for long-term. Real-world: GitHub, Slack, Square all use `gh-ost` for online schema changes and table rebuilds.
**Visual:**
```
Reclaiming InnoDB bloat online:

  Problem: 500GB logical data in 2TB .ibd file (1.5TB dead space)

  Option 1: OPTIMIZE TABLE t;  (MySQL 5.6+ online)
    - ALTER TABLE t ENGINE=InnoDB (rebuild)
    - 5.6+: in-place, concurrent DML allowed
    - Doubles disk usage during rebuild (1.5TB free space needed)
    - Hours on 2TB; risk of long runtime

  Option 2: gh-ost (GitHub Online Schema Change)
    - Create shadow table t_ghost (LIKE t)
    - Copy rows in batches (throttled to avoid load)
    - Capture concurrent changes via binlog (no triggers)
    - Atomic swap: RENAME TABLE t TO t_del, t_ghost TO t
    - No exclusive lock, controllable, resumable
    - Industry standard; used by GitHub, Slack, Square

  Option 3: Page compression
    - ALTER TABLE t ROW_FORMAT=COMPRESSED KEY_BLOCK_SIZE=8;
    - Compresses pages on disk; 500GB logical may shrink to 200GB
    - CPU cost on every read/write (decompress/compress)

  Option 4: MyRocks
    - Different storage engine (RocksDB LSM-tree)
    - 2-10x smaller than InnoDB
    - Migration: dump/restore or row-by-row via binlog
    - Used by Facebook; complex operationally

  Recommended: gh-ost for online rebuild; evaluate compression/MyRocks later
```

### Q4. You want CDC (Change Data Capture) from MySQL to a data warehouse. How do you architect?
**Answer:** MySQL's binlog is the gold standard for CDC — every row change is in the binlog (ROW format), parseable in real time. Architecture: (1) **Enable binlog in ROW format** — `binlog_format=ROW`, `binlog_row_image=FULL` (capture before+after images for updates). (2) **Debezium** — open-source CDC connector that tails the MySQL binlog, parses events, and publishes them to Kafka. Each table becomes a Kafka topic; each row change becomes a Kafka message with `before`/`after`/`op` fields. (3) **Kafka** — durable buffer between MySQL and downstream consumers. Decouples OLTP from analytical load. (4) **Sink connectors** — Kafka Connect sinks stream from Kafka to Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Elasticsearch, etc. (5) **Schema registry** — Avro or Protobuf schemas for the Kafka messages, evolved compatibly. (6) **Snapshot** — initial load of the existing MySQL data into the warehouse (Debezium supports this), then continuous CDC stream. Trade-offs: (1) Binlog in ROW format is large (every column of every changed row) — binlog storage and network bandwidth matter. (2) Debezium stores its binlog position in Kafka Connect offsets; if it falls behind, MySQL must retain binlogs until it catches up (`binlog_expire_logs_seconds`). (3) Schema changes (ALTER TABLE) require careful handling — the schema registry must evolve. (4) Exactly-once semantics are hard — Debezium provides at-least-once; downstream sinks must dedup. Real-world: Netflix uses Debezium + MySQL -> Kafka -> Snowflake for their analytics pipeline; LinkedIn, Uber, and most large companies have similar architectures.
**Visual:**
```
MySQL CDC pipeline (Debezium + Kafka + Snowflake):

  MySQL Primary (binlog_format=ROW, binlog_row_image=FULL)
       |
       | binlog stream
       v
  Debezium connector (tails binlog, parses events)
       |
       | Avro messages (per-table Kafka topic)
       v
  Kafka (durable buffer, schema registry)
       |
       +---> Snowflake sink (Kafka Connect) -> Snowflake (analytics)
       +---> Elasticsearch sink -> ES (search index)
       +---> Redis sink -> Redis (cache invalidation)
       +---> Other consumers (microservices)

  Topic: mysql.users
    {"before":{"id":42,"email":"a@x.com","balance":1000},
     "after": {"id":42,"email":"a@x.com","balance":900},
     "op":"u","ts_ms":1710000000}

  Trade-offs:
    + binlog ROW format is large (every column of changed row)
    + Debezium must keep up or MySQL retains binlogs indefinitely
    + schema changes (ALTER) need schema registry evolution
    + exactly-once is hard; at-least-once + dedup downstream
```

### Q5. Your MySQL queries that used to take 10 ms now take 500 ms after a data load. Diagnose.
**Answer:** Sudden query slowdown after a data load suggests statistics are stale or the working set no longer fits in the buffer pool. Diagnosis: (1) **Check `EXPLAIN`** — has the query plan changed? Common: a `ref` (index lookup) became `ALL` (seq scan) because the index's cardinality dropped after the data load (e.g., a foreign key column where most rows now have the same value). (2) **Run `ANALYZE TABLE`** — MySQL's statistics are estimates; after a large data load, the estimates are stale. `ANALYZE TABLE t` refreshes them. (3) **Check buffer pool hit ratio** — `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS` shows buffer pool hit rate. If it dropped from 99 % to 70 %, the working set no longer fits in `innodb_buffer_pool_size`; queries now hit disk (slow). (4) **Check buffer pool size** — `innodb_buffer_pool_size` should be 50-75 % of RAM on a dedicated MySQL box. If the data grew from 50 GB to 200 GB but the buffer pool is 16 GB, you're now disk-bound. (5) **Check for index bloat** — InnoDB indexes can bloat from page splits on random inserts. (6) **Check for locks** — `SHOW PROCESSLIST` shows blocked queries; a long-running transaction may be holding locks. (7) **Check the query cache** — MySQL 8.0 removed it, but on 5.7 and earlier, the query cache can degrade under high write load (cache invalidation churn). Disable it. Fixes: (1) Run `ANALYZE TABLE` on affected tables (free, fast). (2) Increase `innodb_buffer_pool_size` or move to a bigger instance. (3) Add missing indexes for new query patterns. (4) Kill long-running transactions. (5) Consider partitioning the table. Real-world: the most common cause is stale statistics after a data load; `ANALYZE TABLE` fixes 80 % of cases instantly.
**Visual:**
```
MySQL slow query diagnosis after data load:

  1. EXPLAIN the slow query -> plan changed?
     - ref (index lookup) -> ALL (seq scan)?
     - index cardinality dropped after data load?
     - -> run ANALYZE TABLE t; (refresh stats)

  2. Buffer pool hit ratio?
     SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
     - "Buffer pool hit rate" should be > 99%
     - dropped to 70%? -> working set > buffer pool size
     - fix: increase innodb_buffer_pool_size (or bigger instance)

  3. innodb_buffer_pool_size big enough?
     - should be 50-75% of RAM on dedicated MySQL box
     - data grew 50GB -> 200GB, buffer pool 16GB? -> disk-bound now

  4. Index bloat from page splits?
     - random inserts on non-auto-increment PK -> page splits -> bloat
     - fix: rebuild index (gh-ost online)

  5. Locks? SHOW PROCESSLIST
     - long-running txn holding locks? -> kill, set max_execution_time

  6. Query cache (5.7 and earlier)?
     - high write load -> cache invalidation churn -> disable query_cache

  Most common fix: ANALYZE TABLE (statistics stale after data load)
```

### Q6. You're choosing between MySQL InnoDB Cluster and traditional primary/replica + Orchestrator. How do you decide?
**Answer:** The choice depends on consistency requirements, failover speed, write throughput, and cross-region needs. **Choose InnoDB Cluster if:** (1) You need automatic failover in seconds (Group Replication detects and promotes in 10-30s). (2) You need strong consistency (every committed transaction is consensus-replicated; no data loss, no replica lag for committed data). (3) You need read scale within a single region (Router distributes reads). (4) You have <10 nodes (Group Replication limit). (5) Members are in the same region (low latency, <5ms). **Choose traditional primary/replica + Orchestrator if:** (1) You need cross-region DR (Group Replication can't span regions; consensus too slow). (2) You need very high write throughput (consensus serializes writes; async primary can write faster). (3) You need many replicas (100s of read replicas — Group Replication caps at 9). (4) You need semi-sync (Group Replication's consistency is different — full consensus vs semi-sync receipt ack). (5) You need flexible replication topologies (chain, star, multi-source). Hybrid: use InnoDB Cluster per region for HA, with traditional async cross-region replication for DR. Real-world: most large deployments use the hybrid approach — InnoDB Cluster (or Group Replication) per region, with async cross-region replication. Slack runs Vitess (not InnoDB Cluster) because they need horizontal sharding at scale; InnoDB Cluster doesn't shard. Trade-off: InnoDB Cluster is simpler operationally (one product, automatic failover), but is capped at single-region, <10 nodes, lower write throughput.
**Visual:**
```
InnoDB Cluster vs Traditional + Orchestrator:

  InnoDB Cluster:
    + automatic failover (10-30s)
    + strong consistency (Paxos consensus)
    + read scale via MySQL Router
    - max 9 members
    - single-region (low-latency consensus)
    - lower write throughput (consensus serializes)
    - no sharding (use Vitess for that)

  Traditional + Orchestrator:
    + cross-region DR (async replication)
    + very high write throughput
    + 100s of read replicas
    + flexible topologies
    - failover is slower (Orchestrator, 30s-2min)
    - consistency = semi-sync at best (some lag)
    - more moving parts (Orchestrator, etcd, ProxySQL)

  Decision:
    Need auto-failover + strong consistency + single-region? -> InnoDB Cluster
    Need cross-region DR + very high throughput?             -> Traditional
    Need horizontal sharding?                                -> Vitess
    Need both? -> hybrid: InnoDB Cluster per region + async cross-region
```

### Q7. Your team uses MySQL but needs to add vector search for a RAG feature. What are your options?
**Answer:** MySQL doesn't have native vector types (as of MySQL 8.0; MySQL 9.0 has some vector support but it's early). Options: (1) **OpenSearch / Elasticsearch with binlog CDC** — run a separate vector index in OpenSearch, sync via Debezium binlog CDC. The app queries OpenSearch for vector similarity, fetches full row from MySQL. Decouples vector search from OLTP. (2) **pgvector on PostgreSQL** — migrate the vector-bearing tables to PostgreSQL with pgvector; use MySQL for the rest. Adds operational complexity (two databases) but pgvector is mature. (3) **Dedicated vector DB (Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus)** — sync via CDC or app-level dual-write; best for billion-scale vectors. (4) **MySQL 9.0+ `VECTOR` type** — MySQL 9.0 (2024) added a `VECTOR` data type and `DISTANCE()` function, but no HNSW index yet — brute-force distance computation is too slow for >10k vectors. Watch this space. (5) **Application-level vector search** — load vectors into memory in the app, use a library like FAISS or HNSWLIB. Simple but doesn't scale beyond what fits in RAM. (6) **Hybrid: store vectors as BLOBs in MySQL, sync to a vector index** — vectors are durable in MySQL (with the relational data), but search happens in a separate index (Redis with RediSearch, OpenSearch, or in-app FAISS). Recommended for most teams: option 1 (OpenSearch + CDC) for maturity, or option 6 (Redis RediSearch + BLOBs in MySQL) for simplicity. Real-world: many MySQL shops use OpenSearch + Debezium CDC for search, including vector search; the operational pattern is well-established.
**Visual:**
```
Adding vector search to a MySQL-based app:

  Option 1: OpenSearch + Debezium CDC (mature, decoupled)
    MySQL (vectors as JSON/BLOB) --CDC--> OpenSearch (HNSW index)
    App: vector search in OpenSearch -> fetch row from MySQL
    + mature, scales to billions of vectors
    - new system to operate, eventual consistency on CDC

  Option 2: pgvector migration
    Migrate vector tables to PostgreSQL + pgvector
    + native, in-transaction, HNSW index
    - two databases to operate, migration cost

  Option 3: Dedicated vector DB (Pinecone/Weaviate/Milvus)
    Sync via CDC or app dual-write
    + billion-scale, optimized
    - most operational complexity

  Option 4: MySQL 9.0+ VECTOR type (early, no HNSW yet)
    CREATE TABLE docs (id INT, embedding VECTOR(1536));
    SELECT id, DISTANCE(embedding, ?) AS d FROM docs ORDER BY d LIMIT 10;
    + native, in-transaction
    - no HNSW index yet -> brute force, slow >10k vectors
    - watch this space (likely mature in MySQL 10+)

  Option 5: In-app FAISS/HNSWLIB
    Load vectors into app memory, search in-process
    + simple, no new infra
    - limited to RAM size, no persistence story

  Option 6: MySQL BLOBs + Redis RediSearch
    Vectors as BLOBs in MySQL (durable with relational data)
    Sync to Redis (RediSearch HNSW index) via CDC or dual-write
    + simple, Redis is likely already in stack
    - Redis is in-memory (cost), rebuild on restart

  Recommended: Option 1 (OpenSearch+CDC) or Option 6 (Redis)
```

options: With AFTER_SYNC (lossless) semi-sync, the primary waits for the replica to ack receipt of the binlog event BEFORE committing locally.

MySQL InnoDB doesn't release disk space back to the OS when rows are deleted — it marks the space as free for reuse, but the file stays the same size.

quiz.explanation: In InnoDB, the table's primary key IS the data — rows are stored in the leaves of a B+Tree ordered by PK. This is called a "clustered index." Secondary indexes (on email, created_at, etc.) don't point to the row directly; they store the PK value, so a secondary-index lookup requires two B+Tree descents: (1) find the PK by the secondary key, (2) find the row by PK in the clustered index.
